newsitem.title: GEORGIA: South Ossetian leader elected president.
newsitem.headline: South Ossetian leader elected president.

text.p: South Ossetian leader Lyudvig Chibirov has been elected president of the breakaway region in Georgia, the self-proclaimed state's Central Elections Commission said on Monday.

Incomplete returns from Sunday's election showed the 64-year old ethnographer, who has ruled for three years without the title of president, had won more than 50 percent of the votes in a poll branded illegal by Tbilisi.

The election commission's chief, Boris Chochiyev, said Chibirov had 52.3 percent of the votes counted so far and that this was enough to guarantee victory even though results were not yet in from a few isolated regions.
"In some villages there have been snowstorms and we've lost contact with them, but we believe Chibirov has won in them too," he told Reuters by telephone.

Chiborov had needed more than 50 percent to achieve a first round victory and prevent a second-round run-off. Chibirov's nearest rival, 51-year old philosophy professor Gerasim Khugayev, got 22.9 percent. Others trailed far behind.

South Ossetia, a chunk of territory about the size of Luxembourg, declared independence as the Soviet Union was disintegrating in 1991 and Georgia was gripped by a wave of nationalism which minority groups feared.
Clashes between ethnic Ossetians, an ancient ethnic group whose members speak a language related to Farsi, and Georgians turned into war in 1991.

Late Georgian nationalist President Zviad Gamsakhurdia sent in armed forces in an abortive attempt to crush the independence drive. Fighting with Ossetian volunteers killed more than 1,000 people and left thousands more homeless.

Chibirov, candidate of the South Ossetian Communist Party which dominates the rugged mountainous region's political life, has ruled since 1993 and engineered recent moves to find a peaceful settlement with the Georgian government.

Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze on Monday condemned the vote as "not legal", but said he hoped that peace moves would continue. He has vowed to reunite his Caucasus country which has been plagued by separatism since independence.
Political observers say that, despite the official protests, Georgia is probably relieved to see Chibirov remaining in power.

Economic woes, rising crime in the region and the slim chance that any country will recognise South Ossetia have led Chibirov to seek compromises with Tbilisi, even though he still pays lip service to independence.
Georgia and South Ossetia signed a preliminary political accord earlier this year.

"The government has put a lot at stake in its relationship with Chibirov and he has seemed cooperative. This probably explains the muted response," said Dr Georgi Khutsishvili, Director of Georgia's Centre for Conflict Research.
Chibirov said he was ready at any time to continue negotiations with Tbilisi over South Ossetia's status.
Chochiyev said 61.3 percent of the electorate had turned out, but that some returns had not yet come in from remote mountain areas where inclement whether had knocked out communications.
Most ethnic Georgians have fled the region but several thousand who still live in scattered villages did not take part.
Chibirov, who currently holds the post of Chairman of Parliament, led a battle to create the post of president because he said it was needed to end political infighting.
"Right now the concentration of power in a single person's hands is needed," he told Reuters on Sunday.
